fields.meta_title: Automated Inventory Management That Reorders | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build automated inventory management that drafts reorders, keeps one count across channels, runs cycle counts, and ships expiring lots first.
fields.h1: Build Automated Inventory Management That Reorders on Time
fields.hero_description: Build automated inventory management that drafts reorders at your reorder points and keeps stock in a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into Your Stock Records
fields.features_subheading: Each part handles one job on your stock, and every change lands in the same item record.
fields.feature_1:
A reorder drafted at the reorder point

Set a reorder point and a reorder quantity for each product. When a sale takes stock below that point, the app drafts the reorder and holds it for the buyer to approve.
fields.feature_2:
One count for the shop and the website

Connect your point-of-sale system and your store platform through their APIs. A sale on either channel comes off one shared count before the next customer checks out.
fields.feature_3:
Weekly cycle counts on a phone or tablet

The app picks the bins to count each week. Counters may fix a small variance you set on the spot, and a wider gap goes to the inventory lead with both figures shown.
fields.feature_4:
Lot numbers and expiry dates on receipt

Receiving staff enter the lot and expiry date as cases arrive. A weekly report finds lots close to expiry and lifts them up the pick list, and older stock ships first.
fields.feature_5:
Low-stock alerts in Slack or email

Choose the products that matter and the level that worries you. The app sends a Slack, email, or in-app alert when one crosses it, and a reminder if nobody acts within a day.
fields.feature_6:
Stock history in a database you own

Sales, receipts, counts, and adjustments are written to one history per item. That history sits in a database you own, ready to query for any product in any month you pick.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Jobs the App Runs on Your Stock
fields.tab_content_1:
Below 120 candles, a reorder for 600 waits for the buyer

Tallowmere Gifts sets a reorder point of 120 for its Amber Cedar 8 oz candle. A Thursday sale left 114 on hand, and the app drafted a reorder of 600 candles from Brackenridge Candle Works. The draft waits for Odile Fairweather, the buyer, to approve it before it goes to the supplier.
fields.tab_content_2:
The register and the website both show 133 tubes

Quillon Bike Supply sells inner tubes in its shop and on its website from one shared count. Saturday opened with 200 tubes. The register sold 26 and the online store sold 41, and each sale came off the same count. At close, both channels showed 133 tubes.
fields.tab_content_3:
Bin C-14 counts 5 short and goes to the inventory lead

Harrowgate Pet Supply counts 20 bins every Tuesday. Counters fix gaps of 2 or fewer on the spot and the fix is logged, and a bin off by more than 2 goes to the inventory lead. This week 16 matched and 3 were fixed. Bin C-14 was 5 short, with 31 dog leashes against a record of 36, and went to Ines Okonjo, the lead.
fields.tab_content_4:
312 cases of oat milk move to the top of the pick list

Kestrel Valley Foods tracks oat milk by lot. The Monday report found 4 lots that expire within 30 days: 96 cases of Original, 80 of Barista, 72 of Unsweetened, and 64 of Vanilla. The app moved all 312 cases to the top of the pick list and sent Marisol Achterberg, the sales lead, a direct message.

fields.howto_description: Seven steps to set up automated inventory management with clean item data and clear rules, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Set a reorder point for each product
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Connect the systems that move stock
fields.howto_step_1_des: Export your item list with one row per SKU: name, supplier, unit cost, and the count on hand today. Merge duplicates and retire items you no longer sell. Fix it before anything else: every rule later depends on it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: For each product, write down the reorder point and the quantity you order. Start from what you sell while the supplier's order is on its way, add a buffer you are comfortable with, and mark products you never let run out.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Note each system that records units coming in or going out, starting with your point-of-sale system. Connect each one through its API. A sale or a delivery then changes the same count wherever it happens.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide which reorders the app may send on its own and which wait for the buyer. Name the person who gets count variances and expiry alerts, and the channel each alert uses.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the app in a prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Write the rules from the last four steps in plain English, one paragraph per job, and Emergent builds the app with its database and screens. Change any rule later by prompting again.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Load last month's sales and receipts and run them through the app. Compare the reorders it would have drafted with the ones you placed by hand, and adjust any reorder point that fired too early or too late.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Go live with one category first, such as the 50 items you sell fastest, and count those bins every week for a month. Add the next category when the counts and the reorders hold steady for 4 weeks in a row.

faq_plan.q: What is an automated inventory management system?
faq_plan.ref: What is an automated inventory management system?

prov.original: What is an automated inventory management system?

faq_plan.a: An automated inventory management system is software that keeps stock counts current from the sales and deliveries it records, then acts on rules you set. It drafts a reorder when a product falls below its reorder point and flags bins whose counts do not match. People step in only for the approvals and exceptions those rules send them.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up automated inventory management?
faq_plan.a: Start with a clean item list and a reorder point for every product. Then connect each system where stock changes, such as the register and the store platform, and decide which reorders need a person to approve them. In Emergent's AI automation builder, you describe those rules in plain English and get a working inventory app with its own database.

faq_plan.q: What should inventory automation handle first in a small business?
faq_plan.a: Start with reorders on your fastest-selling products. Their reorder points are the easiest to check against last month's sales, and a missed one is the easiest to spot. Once those drafts look right, add one shared count across your sales channels, then weekly cycle counts. Leave forecasting for later, once you have a few months of clean stock history.

faq_plan.q: What should I look for in automated inventory management software?
faq_plan.a: Look for automated inventory management systems that read sales from every channel you sell on and take a reorder level per product. If you track lots or bins, check those too, and ask how your stock history comes out. If inventory is one part of a wider ecommerce automation plan, orders and stock should share one record. With Emergent, that data lives in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How does automated inventory tracking update stock when an order comes in?
faq_plan.a: It takes the ordered units off the product's count when the store platform reports the order, and puts them back if the order is canceled. Each change is saved with its source and time, and any count can be traced back through those changes. When an order takes a product below its reorder point, that same update starts the reorder.

faq_plan.q: Can I automate inventory management without barcode scanners?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Sales already arrive as records from your register and store platform, and deliveries can be checked in against the supplier's packing list. For cycle counts, staff can type the count for each bin into a form on a phone or tablet. Emergent builds that count form with the rest of the app from a prompt. Add scanners later if typing slows the team down.

faq_plan.q: How does automated inventory management handle stock in two warehouses?
faq_plan.a: It keeps a separate count for each warehouse and a total across both. A rule you set decides which warehouse fills each order, such as the one closer to the customer. A transfer shows up as stock leaving one count and arriving in the other. Pair it with shipping automation, and the label prints at the warehouse that holds the units.

faq_plan.q: How do I set reorder points in an automated inventory system?
faq_plan.a: Set each reorder point at the units you sell during the supplier's lead time, plus a buffer. If you sell 30 a day and the supplier takes 5 days to deliver, that is 150 units before the buffer. Review the points every quarter, and raise them ahead of a season you already know is busy.

faq_plan.q: How often should I run cycle counts once my inventory is automated?
faq_plan.a: Count your fastest-moving and most valuable items every week or two, and everything else once a month or once a quarter. Split the bins so each week's list takes under an hour. Count more often in any area where gaps keep turning up, and less often where counts have matched the record for months.

faq_plan.q: Can an automated inventory management system draft purchase orders on its own?
faq_plan.a: Yes. When stock dips under a product's reorder point, the app drafts a purchase order for the reorder quantity to that product's supplier. The buyer gets a Slack or email alert to approve it. The drafts can also feed procurement automation, where budgets and supplier quotes are checked. Keep a person on the approval for any new supplier.

This page shows the app that runs four concrete jobs on stock: a reorder drafted when a product falls below its reorder point, one count shared by the shop register and the online store, a weekly cycle count with a variance rule, and a Monday report that ships expiring lots first. The FAQ answers what to automate first, how to choose, how to set reorder points and how often to count, as plain operator advice with no accuracy promises.
